conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived—something we do with every new parent. We’ll use a short tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s just 10 questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot anything from normal baby-blues to signs of depression or anxiety so we can give you the right support. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. Feel free to be honest; there are no right or wrong answers. Ready for the first question?  

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[pauses, then gives a small shrug]

It’s… not impossible, but I have to work at it. I used to laugh easily—my husband will make a joke and I’ll smile, maybe chuckle, but it feels kind of forced. Most of the time I’m too tired or distracted by the baby to find things genuinely funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[takes a slow breath]

I guess I’d say “yes, sometimes.” I can still laugh—like, my partner made me giggle about the diaper explosion story—but it’s definitely harder. Things that would’ve cracked me up before now feel kind of muted, like I’m watching myself react instead of just reacting. So it’s not gone completely, just… harder to get there.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[glances down at my hands]

Most days I can still find little things to look forward to—like when my mom’s coming over so I can take a shower without rushing, or the baby’s bedtime stretch that might give me two straight hours of sleep. But the bigger “fun” stuff people keep suggesting—coffee with friends, even leaving the house—feels more like a chore to gear up for than something I actually anticipate. So I guess I still get flashes of excitement, just way fewer and smaller than before.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quietly]

Yeah... a few times this week. The baby had a really fussy night and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or I wasn't holding her right, or I'd done something during the day to throw her off. My head knows babies just cry, but in the moment I catch myself thinking, "This is probably my fault somehow." It's not constant, but it pops up more than I'd like.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[sighs, shifts in the chair]

Yes… mostly at night when the house is quiet. My mind races about everything—her breathing, whether she’s gaining enough weight, if the swaddle is too tight. Sometimes I’ll check her three, four times just to be sure. There’s no real reason, but the worry just sits there like a knot in my chest until I finally drift off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrings hands a little]

A couple of times, yeah. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart races, I feel shaky, and I imagine something awful happening to the baby even though she’s right there sleeping. It passes pretty quickly, maybe a minute or two, but it leaves me jittery for a while. I can’t point to a real reason; it just shows up out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a slow breath]

Yeah… more days than not. Between the feedings, the laundry pile, trying to remember if I ate—some mornings it feels like I’m already behind before I open my eyes. Yesterday I just sat on the couch after everyone left and stared at the mess, thinking, “Where do I even start?” I usually manage to push through, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water most of the week.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[rubs my eyes]

Not exactly. I mean, I do have trouble sleeping, but it’s more that I’m tense and wound up than desperately unhappy. Once the baby finally settles, my body won’t switch off—my mind keeps replaying little worries or to-do lists. I’ll lie there for an hour, sometimes two, before I drift off. It’s frustrating, but it feels more like restlessness than being overcome with sadness.
I have felt sad or miserable

[shrugs a little, eyes on the floor]

I guess “yes, sometimes” fits. There are stretches—usually late afternoon—when this heavy feeling just sort of settles in. I might tear up for no real reason, or feel like I’m moving through fog. It’s not all day, and I still have okay moments, but those waves of sadness catch me off guard a few times this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[shakes head slowly]

No… I haven’t cried like that. My eyes might sting when I’m especially tired, but I haven’t reached the point where the sadness spills over into actual tears. It’s more this dull ache inside than a real crying spell.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[looks up quickly]

No, not at all. I’ve never had thoughts like that—never even crossed my mind. I just want to feel like myself again so I can take care of her.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy-laughter comes only with effort, excitement is limited to small comforts like a shower, and late afternoons bring waves of sadness and worry that leave you feeling overwhelmed. You're working hard to care for your baby and keep the household running, but you feel as though you're barely treading water, and nighttime brings racing thoughts and sudden panicky moments that pass quickly yet leave you jittery.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient still experiences brief flashes of enjoyment but "way fewer and smaller than before," aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "some of the time" with specific examples of unnecessary guilt about baby's crying</sym>, <sym>"Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic episodes that occur repeatedly, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping most days, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring waves of sadness, tearfulness, and fog-like heaviness several times this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 15 places you above the ≥14 cut-off where <med>postpartum depression</med> is probable. You describe core symptoms consistent with <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest (<quote>laughter feels muted</quote>), guilt (<quote>I must have done something wrong</quote>), low mood most days, and functional difficulty. Frequent nocturnal worry and sudden panic symptoms also suggest co-occurring <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to review these results
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation and treatment planning
3. Begin simple mood self-care: 15 minutes of outdoor daylight daily, balanced snacks every 3-4 hours, and accept help with night feeds when possible
4. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or progressive muscle relaxation when panic sensations start; keep a log to discuss with your clinician
5. Share this screening with trusted family so they can support appointments and household tasks while you recover
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale–style interview, self-report.

Symptoms / concerns endorsed:  
- Anhedonia: reduced ability to experience pleasure; laughter feels “muted,” anticipatory enjoyment limited to basic needs (shower, brief sleep).  
- Low mood: late-afternoon “waves” of sadness, foggy feeling, occasional tearfulness without crying spells.  
- Excessive guilt: attributes infant fussiness to personal failings (“I must have done something wrong”).  
- Anxiety: nocturnal racing thoughts, repeated checking of infant; discrete 1–2-min panic episodes (tachycardia, trembling, catastrophic imagery) with no clear trigger.  
- Subjective overwhelm: “barely keeping head above water,” difficulty prioritizing tasks.  
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia secondary to rumination; not perceived as mood-driven.  
- Functional impact: reports “pushing through” daily infant care; no impairment in basic safety or self-care.

Patterns: Symptoms fluctuate but present “more days than not”; worst in late afternoon/night; no correlation with infant’s actual well-being.

Screening significance:  
- Meets partial criteria for mild–moderate postpartum depression (anhedonia, mood lability, guilt, functional strain).  
- Postpartum anxiety features prominent (nocturnal worry, panic attacks).  
- No neurovegetative signs (appetite/weight not mentioned; no daytime tearfulness).  
- No self-harm ideation; no suicidal or infanticidal thoughts stated → safety risk currently absent.

Risk factors noted: Primiparous status, sleep fragmentation, high self-expectations (motherhood performance).

Overall screening impression: Probable mild–moderate postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; safety maintained; warrants further evaluation with standardized EPDS and clinical interview to clarify diagnosis and determine support/intervention needs.
